Going out at night or being outside after dark
Any form of physical contact with others

vignette:
Kwame was nineteen when he was taken. He had been working as a detective for less than a year when a routine undercover operation went wrong and he ended up blindfolded in a basement for three days. His captors rarely spoke, and when they did their voices were low and deliberate, reverberating off concrete walls. They handled him roughly-shoving him, tying his wrists, once gripping his jaw to force water down his throat. He could feel the pressure of their hands long after they let go.

In the weeks following his rescue, Kwame found that the experience lived in him as a series of fragments that refused to assemble into a story. He knew what had happened-the blindfold, the cold floor, the whispers-but when he tried to tell his girlfriend or his partner on the force, the words vanished. He would open his mouth and nothing came out, or he would say "I was in a room" and stop, because that wasn't it at all. The inability to find language for what he'd been through began to feel like its own kind of trap, and so he stopped trying. He decided it was better not to think about it at all. He started actively pushing any thought of the basement away as soon as it surfaced.

But the memories didn't always come as thoughts. Sometimes he would be driving home from a late shift, the dashboard light dim, and he would hear them-the low murmur of his captors' voices, as if they were in the back seat. He knew it wasn't real, yet he would pull over, his heart hammering, and wait for the sound to fade. Other times the fear arrived without any image or sound at all. He would be sitting at his desk reviewing case files and suddenly his entire body would be flooded with the same helpless panic he had felt when the blindfold was first tied, even though nothing in the room resembled that moment. He couldn't explain it, and that made it worse.

These intrusions-the auditory recalls, the wordless waves of emotion-drove him deeper into avoidance. Night became unbearable. He had always worked evening shifts as a detective, but now he requested only day assignments and, when denied, called in sick. His girlfriend noticed he stopped leaving the apartment after dark. He told her he was tired. Physical touch, too, became impossible. When she reached for his hand, he flinched. When she hugged him, he felt the same visceral dread that had come with the stranger's grip on his jaw. He began to stay on his side of the bed, and she stopped reaching.

Kwame knew his strategies were costing him. His captain had noticed his refusal to do night surveillance and had written him up twice for missing assignments. His girlfriend had started sleeping in the guest room. His partner, a veteran detective, had pulled him aside and asked if he was "all there." But every time Kwame considered talking about it, the memory gap opened-a white space where the story should be-and the effort of finding words felt harder than staying silent. So he kept pushing the memories down, kept avoiding the dark, kept dodging hands. It was a cycle he could not name, only feel tightening. What finally brought him to the clinic was his girlfriend's ultimatum: get help or she would leave. That night, alone in his apartment, he heard the captors' voices again and knew he could not carry this alone anymore.
